The following peak device-memory measurements used an A100 with JAX 0.11.2, photometry and a 600-pixel spectrum. Nested-sampling settings were num_live=500, num_delete=100 and the lanes slice kernel. Memory was measured with peak_bytes_in_use.

model parameters peak device memory stellar only 7 2.75 GB + nebular emission, IGM 9 2.87 GB + dust emission 12 2.91 GB

These configurations fit on an 8 GB card. Memory use grows approximately linearly with batch size. The compiled nebular log-likelihood and gradient use 0.81 GB for 100 parameter vectors and 4.3 GB for 500; adding dust emission increases those figures to 0.94 and 4.8 GB.

docs.title: 2. FSPS and $SPS_HOME
docs.text:
CERIDWEN reads the CLOUDY grids (nebular/), dust-emission templates (dust/dustem/) and emission-line list (data/emlines_info.dat) from the FSPS data tree at $SPS_HOME. A fit needs these files but does not run FSPS, so cloning the 3.4 GB repository is sufficient; you do not need to compile it.

export SPS_HOME="$HOME/fsps"
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/cconroy20/fsps.git "$SPS_HOME"

Choose any location for $SPS_HOME. Add that path to your shell startup file:

echo 'export SPS_HOME="$HOME/fsps"' >> ~/.zshrc    # zsh, the macOS default
echo 'export SPS_HOME="$HOME/fsps"' >> ~/.bashrc   # bash, most Linux

Open a new terminal and check that echo $SPS_HOME prints the path.

docs.title: 3. Check the installation
docs.text:
python -m ceridwen.check

The check reports ok, warn or FAIL for each component and suggests fixes for missing dependencies or data. It checks filters, attenuation laws, float64, nested sampling, python-fsps and $SPS_HOME. The python-fsps warning is expected unless you have compiled the wrapper, which is needed only to build a grid.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
fitSED and python -m ceridwen.check check PyPI for newer releases at most once a day. Results are cached in ~/.ceridwen/update_check.json. The check times out after two seconds and produces no message when the network is unavailable. Set CERIDWEN_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to disable it; it is also disabled when $CI is set. Upgrade with pip install --upgrade ceridwen and see the changelog for changes.

To get an email for each new release, open the GitHub page, click Watch, then Custom, and tick Releases (a free GitHub account is needed).

docs.title: SSP grids
docs.text:
A fit requires an SSP grid in HDF5 format. Published grids are registered by name and hosted on Zenodo at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22937956. fetch_grid downloads a grid to ~/.ceridwen/grids (or $CERIDWEN_GRID_DIR), verifies its SHA-256 on each call and returns its path:

from ceridwen import SSPData
from ceridwen.ssps import fetch_grid, available_grids

print(available_grids(published_only=True))        # name -> description
ssp = SSPData.load(fetch_grid("mist_miles_chab"))
name contents size mist_miles_chab MIST isochrones + MILES spectra, Chabrier IMF 67 MB mist_bpass_v2 BPASS v2 binary populations, Chabrier IMF 62 MB amist_c3k_hr_krou_afe aMIST + C3K, Kroupa IMF, five [α/Fe] planes, for CSPBasis_afe (α/Fe) 612 MB

The two solar-scaled grids include the surviving-mass table used by fitSED and PostProcess for mfrac. The α-enhanced grid has no such table; use mfrac=False. Grids downloaded before the September 2026 re-deposit fail the checksum. Replace them with fetch_grid(name, force=True).

docs.title: Building your own SSP grid
docs.text:
To use another IMF, isochrone set or spectral library, build a grid with FSPS. This requires the compiled python-fsps wrapper and a Fortran compiler. Set $SPS_HOME before installing the wrapper:

brew install gcc                       # macOS (Homebrew); or:
sudo apt-get install gfortran          # Debian/Ubuntu; or:
conda install -c conda-forge gfortran  # any OS, inside your conda env

python -m pip install "fsps>=0.4.4"

from ceridwen import SSPData

ssp = SSPData.from_fsps(imf_type=1, save_to="ssp_data.h5")
# later: ssp = SSPData.load("ssp_data.h5")

from_fsps accepts arguments defining the stellar library and IMF, including imf_type, its parameters and isochrone-phase switches. It rejects dust, SFH, nebular, IGM, redshift and fixed-metallicity arguments because the forward model applies those separately. The file records its isochrones, spectral library, IMF, FSPS version and build arguments. CSPBasis reads the isochrone library from this metadata; ssp.display() shows it.

docs.title: Building this documentation
docs.text:
pip install ".[docs]"
mkdocs build

docs.title: Apple GPU (float32 mode)
docs.text: CERIDWEN uses jax-graft to run on Apple Silicon GPUs through JAX's mtl platform. Apple GPUs do not support float64, so this backend uses float32. The sections below describe installation, numerical differences, performance and unsupported features.

docs.title: Install and run
docs.text:
examples/apple_gpu_mock_fit.ipynb generates mock photometry and a spectrum, fits them with nested sampling on the GPU and compares recovered parameters with their inputs and priors. It takes about three and a half minutes on an M3 Pro. Four other notebooks cover specific observation types:

  • mock_fit_1_photometry.ipynb: photometry only.
  • mock_fit_2_photometry_lines.ipynb: photometry and line fluxes, including gas parameters.
  • mock_fit_3_spectrum.ipynb: a spectrum with per-pixel resolving power, sampled velocity dispersion and emission lines.
  • mock_fit_4_spectrum_photometry.ipynb: a spectrum with a sampled flux scale, constrained by photometry.

On Apple Silicon with macOS 26 and Python 3.12 or newer, pip install ceridwen includes jax-graft. Older Macs and Python 3.11 use the CPU build, as specified by the dependency marker in pyproject.toml. Jax-graft selects the GPU as JAX's default device. Importing CERIDWEN then switches the process to float32 and issues a warning. JAX and tensorflow-probability also issue warnings; see Known limits.

UserWarning: float32 mode: JAX's default backend is the Apple GPU (mtl), which has no float64.
Evidences, gradients and the sampler state are float32 (docs/mac_gpu.md); for a float64 fit
set JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu

python -m ceridwen.check reports:

  [ok  ] jax float64  -- off: float32 mode, chosen because the Apple GPU is JAX's default backend ...
  [ok  ] jax backend  -- mtl (mtl:0): Apple GPU via jax-graft, float32

Each fitSED header reports Device : MTL (mtl:0) and Precision : float32. Result files save these as config/platform ("mtl") and config/precision ("float32").

Environment variables control the device and precision:

Environment Precision Device no variables set; jax-graft installed float32 Apple GPU JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu float64 CPU CERIDWEN_X64=0 (any machine) float32 whatever JAX's default device is CERIDWEN_X64=1 with the GPU as default refused at import set JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu instead

CERIDWEN_X64=0 also enables float32 on CPU or CUDA devices. This is useful for comparing with Mac results. Use float64 when the device supports it unless you need that comparison.

docs.title: Implementation of float32 mode
docs.text:
The forward model, likelihood and samplers use float32 with the adjustments below. These adjustments have no effect in float64. Compared with version 1.0.13, the float64 compiled programs were byte-identical across 21,445 arrays in the T4 check. All 1680 output arrays in scripts/physical_check.py were also identical.

Rescaling observations. A cgs F_nu spectrum can have uncertainties near 1e-31. Squaring these underflows float32, whose smallest normal value is 1.2e-38. Before evaluating sigma², inverse variance or A^T W A, ceridwen.likelihood.observation_data scales each observation's data, uncertainties and calibration vector by a power of two, bringing the median uncertainty close to one. Power-of-two scaling preserves the mantissa. The sampled log-jitter is shifted by ln(scale).

The scaled likelihood differs from the physical-unit likelihood by −ndof ln(scale), constant for each observation. Sampling retains this offset: adding a constant of about 1e6 inside a float32 kernel would reduce ln L resolution to about 0.1. run_sampler and map_fit restore the constant on the host in float64 for reported ln Z, ln L and MAP log-posterior. The values are available as likelihood.float32_rescaling and likelihood.loglike_offset.

Array types. Device arrays use ceridwen.precision.float_dtype(). Host-side NumPy calculations retain float64, including SSP axes, Z_sun resolution, provenance and result-file data.

Numerical range. The ionising-photon table uses a constant L_sun / h = 5.8e59. It is computed on the host in float64 before storage in the working type. The metallicity and dust-emission kernels replace their 1e-70 floors with the smallest normal float32 value.

Float32 mode does not support Spectrum(marginalize_elines=True), whose normal equations use flux units. It also rejects fixed numeric jitter, which cannot be rescaled with the data; use sampled jitter instead.

docs.title: Numerical comparisons
docs.text:
tests/test_float32_parity.py compares six golden configurations and a nine-parameter mock galaxy with SDSS photometry, a 600-pixel cgs spectrum (sigma ~ 1e-31) and three line fluxes. Separate processes evaluate float64 on the CPU, float32 on the CPU and float32 on the GPU. These measurements used an M3 Pro, JAX 0.11.2 and jax-graft 0.0.5 on 15 October 2026:

Quantity float32 vs float64 Metal vs float32 CPU Metal run to run SSP weights W 3e-6 (step) / 5e-6 (linear) of the largest weight 2e-7 identical spectrum, continuum pixels 5e-6 relative 2e-7 identical spectrum, pixels under a nebular line up to 4e-4 relative (4e-5 of the peak) 2e-7 identical photometry (maggies) 2e-5 relative 9e-7 (mock), 3e-5 (golden 15000-pixel integrals) identical line fluxes 4e-6 relative 2e-7 identical ln posterior (true units) 4e-4 and 0.015 on values of 4e4 and 2e4 0.01 identical gradient 5e-5 of the largest component up to 6e-4 relative (three runs: 1e-5, 8e-5, 6e-4)

Line-pixel differences arise from evaluating (lambda - lambda_0) / sigma in float32. Near 1e4 Å, float32 resolves about 1e-3 Å, which shifts the profile wings slightly. CPU float32 shows the same effect.

GPU gradients vary between runs because the transpose of redshift interpolation uses atomic scatter-adds. The forward predictions and ln L were byte-identical between runs in these checks.

The tested float32 posteriors agreed with float64 within sampling variation. Evidence agreement required twice as many inner steps; see Speed. Float32 and float64 outputs differ numerically, and GPU nested-sampling runs with the same rng_key need not be identical.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
scripts/bench_mac_metal.py fits the comparison mock in each precision mode and times value-only likelihood calls at the sampler's batch widths:

python tests/baselines/_capture_f32.py --no-goldens ref.npz
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu                python scripts/bench_mac_metal.py --mock-data ref.npz --out bench/f64_cpu
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu CERIDWEN_X64=0 python scripts/bench_mac_metal.py --mock-data ref.npz --out bench/f32_cpu
                                 python scripts/bench_mac_metal.py --mock-data ref.npz --out bench/f32_mtl
python scripts/bench_mac_metal.py --compare bench/*/summary.json

The benchmark used an M3 Pro, JAX 0.11.2 and jax-graft 0.0.5 on 15 October 2026, with nine free parameters, num_live=200 and num_delete=40. us/point is the median value-only ln L runtime under vmap over 200 calls, excluding compilation:

run inner steps ln Z calls wall us/point W=40 us/point W=200 CPU float64, seed 0 30 40933.16 +- 0.36 168 000 1731 s 1550 1335 CPU float64, seed 1 30 40933.21 +- 0.32 169 200 1879 s CPU float32, seed 0 30 40930.96 +- 0.40 180 000 1017 s 765 750 Metal float32, seed 0 30 40931.88 +- 0.39 176 400 421 s 174 131 Metal float32, seed 1 30 40932.04 +- 0.46 174 000 418 s Metal float32, seed 0 60 40933.77 +- 0.38 328 800 908 s

In this benchmark, GPU likelihood evaluations were 9–10 times faster than float64 CPU evaluations and 4–6 times faster than float32 CPU evaluations. The 30-step GPU fit took about a quarter of the float64 CPU runtime. The sampler's control loop still runs on the CPU.

The evidence estimates were sensitive to inner-step count in float32. The two float64 seeds differed by 0.05 in ln Z. With 30 inner slice steps, float32 estimates on both devices were 1.1–2.2 nats lower, or 3–6 times their quoted errors. With 60 steps, the GPU estimate was 40933.77 ± 0.38, consistent with float64. The float32 slice sampler appears to mix less efficiently per step; the cause is unknown. Peak ln L agreed within 0.3 across runs, while incomplete mixing in nested sampling can bias Z downward.

Posterior means and widths showed similar variation in all six runs. The two float64 runs differed by up to 1.8 standard deviations in their means, with width ratios of 0.3–1.7 at 200 live points. Float32 results fell within this variation.

When comparing evidences, use matching precision, num_live, num_delete and num_inner_steps, and check mixing. In this test, changing precision or doubling the inner steps shifted ln Z by 1–2 nats. fitSED records precision, platform and sampler settings in the result file. The default remains 30 inner steps in both precision modes.

scripts/mac_metal_probe.py compares the values and runtimes of 34 JAX operations on CPU and GPU. All 34 agreed in the comparison; the script prints the results.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Jax-graft 0.0.5 is experimental. Unsupported operations fail during compilation with UNIMPLEMENTED: Metal: .... Include the fitSED header and python -m ceridwen.check output when reporting a failure.
  • Tensorflow-probability requests float64 internally. On the first prior draw, JAX warns that it is truncating those requests to float32, with messages from tfp's random_generators.py, numpy_array.py and ops.py, and JAX's array_methods.py. JAX also prints Platform 'mtl' is experimental .... These warnings are expected. XLA may report slow constant folding for large models; this indicates compilation time rather than a failed fit.
  • The nested-sampling progress bar reports ln Z in scaled units. It may differ from the final value by ndof ln(scale), which can be thousands of nats for a spectrum. The final report and result file use physical units.
  • The nested sampler dispatches its inner loop step by step. Small GPU batches can be slower than CPU batches. Wider batches and gradient-based samplers make better use of the GPU.

docs.title: Noise and calibration
docs.text: By default, the likelihood is Gaussian and uses the uncertainties supplied with each observation. You can add error floors, rescale uncertainties, mark upper limits or fit a spectral calibration. The outlier mixture and GP likelihood are described separately. Section 5 of GOTCHAS.md lists unsupported combinations.

docs.title: Fixed terms, set on the observation
docs.text:
• Spectrum(noise_floor=f): a fractional floor, sigma_eff² = sigma² + (f |model|)².
  • Photometry(upper_limit=mask): bands where mask is True get a one-sided penalty (only a model above the data is penalised).

docs.title: Sampled noise terms
docs.text:
To sample any of the following variance terms, add a prior and a free_param_init entry in SedModel:

parameter variance becomes log_err_scale_<kind> sigma² exp(2 log_err_scale): a common rescaling of the quoted errors log_jitter_<kind> + exp(log_jitter)², in data units log_f_calib_<kind> + (exp(log_f_calib) |model|)² log_f_data_<kind> + (exp(log_f_data) |data|)²

Replace <kind> with phot, spec or lines. For several observations of the same type, use <root>_<kind>_<obs.name>, such as log_jitter_spec_nirspec; the unsuffixed name is then ambiguous and raises an error. Use a constant transform to fix a term.

fitSED reads these names automatically. With run_sampler, construct the DiagonalNoiseModel yourself. log_jitter is the natural log of a flux in the observation's units: maggies, cgs F_nu or erg s⁻¹ cm⁻². Choose its prior relative to the supplied uncertainties.

docs.title: Calibrating a spectrum
docs.text:
A spectrum and photometry may have different flux calibrations. Including photometry constrains the absolute flux scale and helps separate continuum calibration errors from dust and age. Choose one calibration method per spectrum:

  • Sampled calibration. spectrum_scaling multiplies the entire Spectrum prediction. spectrum_calib, a vector of shape (order,), adds a factor 1 + sum_k c_k P_k(x). The P_k are Legendre polynomials, with observed wavelengths mapped to [-1, 1] over all pixels. There is no P_0 term because spectrum_scaling sets the level. For several spectra, use spectrum_scaling_<obs.name> and spectrum_calib_<obs.name>.
  • Profiled polynomial. Spectrum(polynomial_order=M) solves for Chebyshev coefficients c_0..c_M at each likelihood call, as in Prospector's PolyOptCal. The posterior is conditional on the best-fitting polynomial and does not include its uncertainty.
  • Marginalised polynomial. Spectrum(polynomial_order=M, polynomial_mode="marginalize", polynomial_prior_sigma=s) integrates out the coefficients under a Gaussian prior. The width s is in fractional-response units. This propagates calibration uncertainty into the posterior and evidence without adding sampled parameters.

eline_scaling applies only to emission-line fluxes in a Lines observation. It does not scale a Spectrum prediction.

docs.title: Outlier mixture likelihood
docs.text:
Bad pixels, sky residuals and calibration errors can strongly affect a Gaussian fit: a 20σ residual contributes −200 to ln L. The outlier mixture models each datum with either the ordinary noise distribution or, with probability f, a Gaussian nsigma times broader (Hogg, Bovy & Lang 2010, arXiv:1008.4686). It reproduces Prospector's f_outlier > 0 likelihood (prospect.likelihood.NoiseModel) to machine precision.

All f_outlier_* values default to zero. Enable the mixture by sampling a fraction or fixing it above zero. With the fraction absent or fixed at zero, the compiled likelihood is the ordinary Gaussian.

docs.title: The likelihood
docs.text:
For each unmasked datum i, σ_eff,i includes all configured noise terms: noise_floor, log_err_scale_*, log_jitter_*, log_f_calib_* and log_f_data_*. Define χ_i = (y_i − μ_i)/σ_eff,i and log_det_i = ½ ln(2π σ_eff,i²):

ln p_good,i = −½ χ_i²          − log_det_i
ln p_bad,i  = −½ χ_i² / n²     − log_det_i − ln n
ln L_i      = logaddexp( ln(1 − f) + ln p_good,i ,  ln f + ln p_bad,i )
ln L        = Σ_i ln L_i          (masked data contribute 0)

Prospector sets var_bad = var n², giving a broad-component normalisation of −½ ln(2π var) − ln n. Its diagonal Sigma is equivalent to CERIDWEN's σ_eff², including any noise kernels. tests/test_outlier_model.py compares all noise-term combinations with a NumPy transcription at rtol 1e-12 and with Prospector outputs in tests/reference/prospector_outlier.npz.

At exactly f_outlier == 0, Prospector's NoiseModel.lnlikelihood (noise_model.py:90, commit a78d153) instead computes −½[ln(2π) χ² + Σ ln σ²]. This multiplies χ² by ln 2π and omits n ln 2π. CERIDWEN uses the ordinary Gaussian at zero, which is also the limit of its mixture as f → 0. The two implementations therefore differ at f = 0.

docs.title: Using it with fitSED
docs.text:
Configure the fraction by observation name, as with other noise terms. Each observation has a separate fraction.

parameter observation CERIDWEN default Prospector template (reference only, TemplateLibrary["outlier_model"]) f_outlier_spec the Spectrum 0 (off) free, init 0.01, TopHat(1e-5, 0.5) nsigma_outlier_spec the Spectrum 50 fixed at 50 f_outlier_phot the Photometry 0 (off) fixed at 0; TopHat(0.0, 0.5) when freed nsigma_outlier_phot the Photometry 50 fixed at 50 f_outlier_lines the Lines 0 (off) no template (see below) nsigma_outlier_lines the Lines 50 —

These defaults also apply to names with observation suffixes.

For small photometric sets, leaving f_outlier_phot=0 usually gives a better SFR constraint unless a bad band is suspected. In an A100 recovery test with eight clean NIRCam bands, sampling f_outlier_phot with TopHat(0.0, 0.5) gave an SFR median and [16, 84%] interval of 0.592 [−0.344, 0.753], compared with 0.770 [0.580, 0.965] for the Gaussian fit. Treating a rest-UV band as a possible outlier weakened the constraint. More bands are needed to distinguish bad measurements from changes in the SED.

For several observations of one type, include their names. Two spectra named "G140M" and "G395M" use f_outlier_spec_G140M and f_outlier_spec_G395M, with matching nsigma_outlier_spec_<name> keys. The plain f_outlier_spec requires exactly one spectrum. Providing both plain and suffixed names for one observation, or a name matching no observation, raises an error.

To sample a fraction, give it a prior and free_param_init entry. This example enables the mixture for the spectrum while keeping photometry Gaussian:

from ceridwen.priors import TopHat

model = SedModel(csp, [phot, spec],
                 priors={**priors, "f_outlier_spec": TopHat(low=0.0, high=0.5)},
                 free_param_init={**init, "f_outlier_spec": jnp.array([0.01])},
                 transforms=transforms, zred=zred)
result = fitSED(model, output_dir="out")

The fitSED log reports the sampled fraction and fixed width as spec: DiagonalGaussianLikelihood, outlier mixture f = f_outlier_spec (sampled), nsigma = 50 (fixed). Other observations report outlier mixture off.

  • Fix a fraction with a constant transform, for example transforms={"f_outlier_phot": lambda th: jnp.array([0.05])}. Setup checks that the transform is constant. A value of 0 disables the mixture.
  • nsigma_outlier_* defaults to 50. It can be fixed with a transform or sampled with a prior bounded above zero. It requires a matching fraction.
  • Priors on f must be bounded within [0, 1], such as Uniform, TopHat or ClippedNormal.
  • With run_sampler, construct the noise model explicitly: DiagonalNoiseModel(f_outlier="f_outlier_spec", nsigma_outlier=50.0). Strings refer to theta keys; numbers are fixed values.

docs.title: Line fluxes (Lines)
docs.text: Prospector applies the same noise-model likelihood to Lines, though it has no template parameter for the fraction. CERIDWEN calls it f_outlier_lines. With few line fluxes, the fraction is usually prior-dominated. The mixture can still reduce the effect of a mismeasured line, for example from blending or aperture errors. A small fixed fraction, such as 0.05, is often sufficient.

docs.title: Upper limits
docs.text: Upper limits retain the one-sided penalty −½ max(μ − y, 0)²/σ² − log_det. Only detections use the mixture (lnlike_diag_outlier_with_upper_limits). Prospector has no equivalent upper-limit kernel; its outlier branch is the reference for detections only.

docs.title: Emission-line marginalisation
docs.text:
Spectrum(marginalize_elines=True) jointly integrates over line fluxes in that spectrum and all Photometry and Lines observations. The analytic solution requires a Gaussian likelihood. An outlier mixture within this system raises NotImplementedError. A second spectrum outside the marginalisation can use the mixture.

Prospector first fits line amplitudes with the quoted uncertainties (sedmodel.py:324,686, spec_unc=None), ignoring noise kernels. It then adds a Gaussian Occam term and applies the mixture to the spectrum with maximum-likelihood lines. CERIDWEN does not implement this approximation to integration over the line fluxes.

docs.title: The prior at f = 0 and its gradient
docs.text:
The mixture becomes Gaussian at f = 0, so a prior starting at zero includes the no-outlier case. ln L is concave in f and finite at zero. Its derivative is d ln L/df = Σ_i (p_bad,i − p_good,i)/L_i, reducing to Σ_i (p_bad,i/p_good,i − 1) at f = 0. For nsigma=50, this overflows float64 only for residuals beyond roughly 38σ.

CERIDWEN evaluates the derivative directly through the custom JVP _mixture_jvp in ceridwen/likelihood/likelihood.py. Differentiating through ln f at zero would instead produce NaN from 0·∞. The test test_gradient_in_f_is_exact_and_finite_at_zero checks this boundary. Prospector's lower bound of 1e-5 is therefore unnecessary for numerical stability in CERIDWEN. A prior upper bound of 0.5 keeps the ordinary-noise component as the majority.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
With the mixture enabled, LikelihoodOutput.lnl_pointwise contains each datum's ln L_i and sums to lnl_total. chi and residuals still use the ordinary Gaussian residual (y − μ)/σ_eff. To compute each datum's posterior outlier probability, p_i = exp(ln f + ln p_bad,i − ln L_i), use:

p = likelihood.outlier_probability(obs.flux, pred, obs.uncertainty, obs.mask, theta)

This is available through DiagonalGaussianLikelihood.outlier_probability or ceridwen.likelihood.outlier_probability. It is computed only when requested.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• The mixture assumes diagonal noise, as does Prospector's implementation (assert Sigma.ndim == 1). Combining it with a GP likelihood on the same spectrum raises an error at setup.
  • Observations within a joint emission-line marginalisation cannot use the mixture, as described above.

docs.title: Non-finite data
docs.text: At construction, observations mask non-finite fluxes and uncertainties that are non-finite or non-positive. They warn if those points were not already masked. The likelihood substitutes finite placeholders for masked non-finite values so they cannot contaminate values or gradients through 0·NaN. The original obs.flux array is retained.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
For each datum, the mixture evaluates two Gaussians and a logaddexp instead of one Gaussian. An A100 benchmark used a 3065-pixel spectrum, eight bands, nebular emission, sampled fractions for both observation types and 240 interleaved calls. At the nested-sampling batch width W = 100, runtime increased by 0.6% for both value-only and value-and-gradient calculations. Changes at W = 1 and 500 ranged from −0.1% to +0.8%. At W = 4, corresponding to four NUTS chains, value and gradient cost 1.9% more: 49 µs on 2.59 ms.

With the fraction absent or fixed at zero, the lowered StableHLO for jit(value_and_grad(lnprob)) is identical to the likelihood before this feature in all four scripts/bit_identity_check.py configurations.

docs.title: Post-processing a fit
docs.text:
ceridwen.PostProcess evaluates posterior draws using the fitted forward model. It returns sampled parameters, star formation histories, time-averaged SFRs, UV and ionising-photon quantities, and predictions for each observation. It also provides full, stellar-intrinsic and dust-free model-grid spectra, the highest-likelihood sample and any quantities defined by your own functions.

from ceridwen import PostProcess, load_postprocess

pp  = PostProcess(model, result)      # the SedModel of the fit; SamplingResult or the .h5 path
out = pp.run()                        # nested dict of numpy arrays
pp.save("post.npz")                   # flat .npz; load_postprocess("post.npz") rebuilds the dict

Use the same CSP, observations, transforms and zred as in the fit. PostProcess checks parameter names and shapes against the result and reports both lists if they differ. When loading an .h5 file, it also checks the saved fixed redshift, luminosity distance, cosmology and kinematics, including broaden_photometry.

run() evaluates draws with model.predict_vmap. If you have reassigned model.observations, call model.setup_observations() first.

docs.title: Output fields
docs.text:
Key Shape Meaning out['theta'][name] (N,) or (N, k) equal-weight posterior draws of every sampled parameter out['log_likelihood'], out['draw_index'] (N,) log-likelihood of each draw and its index in the raw samples out['extras']['sfh']['lookback_gyr'] (N, n_time) lookback grid of each draw (follows a sampled zred when track_zred_age; the SFR is scaled with it so the formed mass is kept) out['extras']['sfh']['sfr'] (N, n_time) or (N, n_time-1) SFR in M⊙/yr in the CSP's convention (per node, or per bin for sfh_per_bin) out['extras']['sfh']['sfr_per_bin'] (N, n_time-1) the per-bin SFR the step kernel integrates out['extras']['sfh']['mass_formed'] (N,) ∫ SFR dt, M⊙ out['extras']['sfh']['sfr10'], sfr100, ... (N,) mean SFR over the last 10, 100, ... Myr (windows_myr, default 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500) out['extras']['sfh']['ssfr10'], ... (N,) sfrW / mass_formed, 1/yr out['extras']['sfh']['mfrac'] (N,) surviving / formed mass (stars + remnants); only with a grid that carries a mass table (below) out['extras']['sfh']['mass_surviving'] (N,) mfrac * mass_formed, M⊙ out['extras']['sfh']['ssfr10_surviving'], ... (N,) sfrW / mass_surviving, 1/yr out['extras']['uv']['MUV'], LUV (N,) absolute AB magnitude at 1500 Å and mean L_ν over 1450–1550 Å (erg/s/Hz) of the full (dust-attenuated) model out['extras']['uv']['MUV_intrinsic'], LUV_intrinsic (N,) the same from the stellar-intrinsic spectrum out['extras']['ionizing']['nion'] (N,) Q(H) in s⁻¹ from the intrinsic spectrum, with the nebular model's constants out['extras']['ionizing']['xion'] (N,) nion / LUV_intrinsic, Hz/erg out['extras']['ionizing']['fesc'] (N,) frac_obrun, present only when the model has it out['prediction']['photometry'][obs] (N, n_bands) maggies, one entry per Photometry observation out['prediction']['spectra'][obs] (N, n_pix) as the Spectrum observation is fitted out['prediction']['lines'][obs] (N, n_lines) integrated line fluxes out['prediction']['wave_rest'] (n_wave,) the model grid, Å out['prediction']['spectra_observed'], zred (N, n_wave), (N,) observed-frame f_ν in erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² Hz⁻¹ (cgs; × 1e32 for nJy) at (1+z) wave_rest (flux factor and IGM applied; not broadened), and the redshift of each draw; present only when the model has a fixed or sampled zred or a lumdist_mpc (absent for a zred = 0 fit, which has no flux factor) out['prediction']['spectra_model'] (N, n_wave) rest-frame L_ν [L⊙/Hz] of the fitted model (dust, nebular, dust emission; at model resolution, no kinematic broadening), × 10^logmass out['prediction']['spectra_intrinsic'] (N, n_wave) stellar continuum only: no dust, no nebular, ionising continuum included out['prediction']['spectra_dustfree'] (N, n_wave) stars + nebular continuum + lines, no dust out['derived'][name] (N,) or (N, k) your functions (below) out['bestfit'] same tree, one draw the highest-likelihood raw sample, with all of the above out['meta'] n_samples, n_raw, seed, resampled, windows_myr, param_names, zred_fixed, cosmology, sampler, weights (source), log_evidence, log_evidence_err, observations, sfh_interp, sfh_per_bin, metallicity (convention and grid Z_sun), mfrac (read from the file's /derived/mfrac, computed from the grid's table, or not computed)

Disable unneeded outputs with PostProcess(..., sfr=False, ssfr=False, uv=False, ionizing=False, predictions=False, mfrac=False).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Posterior draws. Nested-sampling weights are recomputed from dead-point log-likelihoods and birth contours, using exact live-point counts in sample order (ceridwen.sampler.ns_weights.nested_log_weights). If birth contours are unavailable, stored log_weights are used. A warning reports any difference between stored and recomputed weights; the recomputed values take precedence.

Draws are resampled to equal weight, so ordinary histograms and quantiles describe the posterior. n_samples defaults to 2000, with a fixed seed. NUTS draws already have equal weights; n_samples selects a subset. bestfit is the raw sample with the highest log-likelihood.

Star formation. After transforms, theta['sfh'] contains the SFH shape in the CSP's convention. With logmass, physical SFR is that shape × 10^logmass. The CSP applies mass scaling to the spectrum. Thus logmass represents formed mass when the SFH integrates to one solar mass on the construction grid, as ensured by logsfr_ratios_to_sfh(..., sfh_times_yr=csp.sfh_times). A directly sampled sfh has its own normalisation.

With track_zred_age=True, each draw's grid ends at age(zred) and its SFR is scaled by T_grid / age(zred) to preserve formed mass. sfrW averages the same SFH used by the weight kernel over the last W Myr: constant per bin for sfh_interp="step" and linear between nodes for "linear". SFR is zero beyond the oldest node. ssfrW divides this average by formed mass, without a stellar return correction.

Surviving mass. mfrac is the fraction of formed mass remaining in stars and remnants. It weights the SSP grid's ssp_stellar_mass table by the same SSP weights used for the spectrum. The table stores FSPS's stellar_mass per SSP under schema 3. For MIST ages below about 2.5 Myr, FSPS's lowest IMF bin is counted by mass rather than number; see GOTCHAS section 14. mass_surviving = mfrac * mass_formed and ssfrW_surviving = sfrW / mass_surviving give the Prospector-style mass and sSFR.

The published mist_miles_chab and mist_bpass_v2 grids include this table, and SSPData.from_fsps saves it in new grids. The α-enhanced amist_c3k_hr_krou_afe grid does not include it; use mfrac=False. By default, a missing table produces one warning and only formed mass is reported. mfrac=True instead raises an error; update a published grid with fetch_grid(<name>, force=True) or rebuild a custom grid with from_fsps. mfrac=False skips the calculation without a warning.

A table with surviving masses above 1 M_sun per M_sun formed is rejected with a warning when loaded; the grid remains usable without it. Composite mfrac uses CERIDWEN's SFH integration rather than FSPS's csp_gen. For constant and rising SFHs over 0.1–10 Gyr, agreement with python-fsps is 4.2e-4 for step interpolation and 6.3e-3 for linear interpolation. The larger difference occurs for young MIST populations, whose youngest node is 10^5 yr. See GOTCHAS section 14.

Stored mfrac. When a table is available, fitSED computes mfrac for every stored sample without evaluating spectra. This takes well under a second for thousands of samples. Values are saved in /derived/mfrac, aligned with /samples. Attributes stellar_mass_source, grid_chash and sfh_interp identify the table and integration scheme. You can read stellar masses directly:

from ceridwen import read_result_h5
r = read_result_h5("out/ceridwen_result.h5")
mass_surviving = r["derived"]["mfrac"] * 10 ** r["samples"]["logmass"].ravel()   # per sample, M_sun

Apply the weights in r["samples"]["log_weights"], or use PostProcess to resample. PostProcess(model, "out/ceridwen_result.h5") uses stored mfrac without requiring the mass table, but checks that grid_chash and sfh_interp match the model. Given a SamplingResult, or a file without /derived, it computes mfrac from the grid table.

fitSED(mfrac=False) skips /derived; mfrac=True requires a table before sampling. By default, the array is saved when possible, with one log message otherwise. /derived is reserved for inexpensive, reproducible functions of theta and the model. Spectra, SFR averages, UV properties and ionising quantities are computed by PostProcess.

Model-grid spectra. These are rest-frame luminosity densities, without distance scaling, (1+z) or IGM absorption. Use per-observation predictions when comparing with data.

UV and ionising photons. LUV is the trapezoidal mean of rest-frame L_ν over 1450–1550 Å; MUV = −2.5 log10(LUV / (4π (10 pc)²) / 3631 Jy). nion = (L⊙/h) ∫_{λ<912 Å} L_ν/λ dλ uses the intrinsic spectrum and the constants from NebularGridModel.compute_log_qq. It matches the ionising photon rate used by the fit. xion = nion / LUV_intrinsic, and fesc is the fixed or sampled frac_obrun.

docs.title: Custom quantities
docs.text:
Pass functions in derived to compute additional quantities. Each receives one SpectrumSample and returns a float or 1-D array. Functions run in a Python loop for each draw and the best-fit sample, so avoid expensive work:

import numpy as np

def A_V(s):                                   # V-band attenuation from the two spectra
    i = s.index_of(5500.0)
    return 2.5 * np.log10(s.dustfree[i] / s.full[i])

def L_optical(s):                             # erg/s in 4000-7000 A rest, dust-attenuated
    return s.luminosity(s.full, 4000.0, 7000.0)

def beta_UV(s):                               # UV slope of the full model
    m = (s.wave_rest > 1300) & (s.wave_rest < 2600)
    flam = s.full[m] / s.wave_rest[m] ** 2
    return np.polyfit(np.log10(s.wave_rest[m]), np.log10(flam), 1)[0]

pp = PostProcess(model, result, derived={"A_V": A_V, "L_opt": L_optical, "beta": beta_UV})
out = pp.run()
out["derived"]["A_V"]                         # (N,)
out["bestfit"]["derived"]["A_V"]              # float

SpectrumSample provides wave_rest, full, intrinsic and dustfree (spectra in L⊙/Hz × 10^logmass), transformed NumPy theta, zred, logmass, sfr, lookback_gyr and cosmo. Helpers include index_of(λ), mean_lnu(spec, lo, hi) and luminosity(spec, lo, hi).

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
pp.figures("post_figs/", title="ID 1009077")      # summary.pdf, corner.pdf, diagnostics.pdf

ceridwen.plotting creates three matplotlib figures:

  • Summary: observed-frame SED, data, posterior photometry, 16–84% model band and χ residuals, plus line residuals and S/N when lines are fitted. Without lines, the SED spans the page width. The SFH panel shows per-bin SFR, posterior median and 16–84% interval, the prior interval at median mass and the input SFH when supplied in truths. Uniform time grids use a linear axis; other grids use a log axis. Parameter panels show medians, 16–84% intervals, best-fit values and prior intervals. The header reports z, log M, log SFR10, best-fit χ²/ν and ln Z.
  • Corner: all fitted parameters, with median dashed lines and the maximum-likelihood sample in red.
  • Diagnostics: nested-sampling dead points in deletion order, coloured by posterior weight, with log-likelihood, cumulative posterior weight, ln Z and effective sample size. MCMC results show per-chain traces, split-R̂ and ESS. Without VI, NUTS chains share one warmup end state, so R̂ measures mixing within that run only.

summary_figure(out, model), corner_figure(out) and diagnostic_figure(result, out) return figures you can edit. The default blue palette is defined in plotting.COLORS.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: pp.save("post.npz") writes a flat .npz file with slash-separated keys, such as extras/sfh/sfr10 and bestfit/theta/logmass. Strings and lists in meta are JSON-encoded. load_postprocess(path) restores the nested dictionary.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This example fits a mock galaxy observed in twelve bands from GALEX to WISE and an optical spectrum. The mock uses the same forward model as the fit, so the fitted parameters can be compared with their input values. After installation, run the blocks in order in one Python session.

1. Download an SSP grid. The MIST + MILES grid uses a Chabrier IMF and is 67 MB. fetch_grid caches it in ~/.ceridwen/grids (or $CERIDWEN_GRID_DIR) and checks its SHA-256 on every call. Use available_grids() to list other grids.

from ceridwen import SSPData
from ceridwen.ssps import fetch_grid

ssp = SSPData.load(fetch_grid("mist_miles_chab"))
ssp.display()                                      # library, IMF, grid coverage

2. Build the model. lookback_time contains SFH nodes in Gyr, increasing from 0 at the present. A transform converts the sampled logsfr_ratios into an SFR at each node. logzsol is log10(Z/Z_sun) for the loaded grid.

import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from ceridwen import CSPBasis, SedModel, Instrument, Cosmology
from ceridwen.observation import Photometry, Spectrum
from ceridwen.model import logsfr_ratios_to_sfh
from ceridwen.priors import Uniform, ClippedNormal, StudentT

ZRED = 0.1                                         # fixed spectroscopic redshift
FILTERS = ["galex_FUV", "galex_NUV", "sdss_u0", "sdss_g0", "sdss_r0",
           "sdss_i0", "sdss_z0", "twomass_J", "twomass_H", "twomass_Ks",
           "wise_w1", "wise_w2"]
SPEC_WAVE = np.linspace(4000.0, 8000.0, 600)       # observed-frame vacuum Angstrom
LSF = Instrument.sigma_kms(150.0)                  # instrumental line-spread function

csp = CSPBasis(ssp, lookback_time=jnp.linspace(0.0, 12.0, 6),
               cosmo=Cosmology.planck18(),
               zh_const=True, sfh_interp="step",
               add_dust=False, add_diffuse_dust=True, add_neb=False, verbose=False)

sfh_times_yr = np.array(csp.sfh_times)
def logsfr_to_sfh(free_theta):
    return logsfr_ratios_to_sfh(free_theta["logsfr_ratios"], sfh_times_yr=sfh_times_yr)

def build_model(observations):
    return SedModel(
        csp, observations=observations,
        priors={
            "logzsol": Uniform(low=-2.0, high=0.2),
            "logmass": Uniform(low=9.0, high=12.0),
            "diffuse_tau_kc": ClippedNormal(mean=0.3, sigma=1.0, low=0.0, high=4.0),
            "diffuse_dust_index": Uniform(low=-1.0, high=0.4),
            "logsfr_ratios": StudentT(df=2.0, mean=0.0, scale=0.3),
        },
        transforms={"sfh": logsfr_to_sfh},
        free_param_init={"logsfr_ratios": jnp.zeros(5), "logmass": jnp.array([10.0])},
        zred=ZRED,
    )

By default, SedModel uses a galaxy velocity dispersion of 300 km/s. Change it with kinematics=Kinematics(sigma_gal=...), or fit it by using Kinematics(sigma_gal="sigma_gal") and adding a prior. See Conventions.

3. Generate mock data. Evaluate the model at known parameters and add noise, with signal-to-noise ratios of 20 for photometry and 25 for the spectrum.

TRUTH = {
    "logsfr_ratios":      jnp.array([0.3, 0.2, -0.1, -0.4, -0.6]),
    "logzsol":            jnp.array([-0.2]),
    "logmass":            jnp.array([10.5]),
    "diffuse_tau_kc":     jnp.array([0.5]),
    "diffuse_dust_index": jnp.array([-0.7]),
}
gen = build_model([Photometry(filters=FILTERS, name="phot"),
                   Spectrum(wavelength=SPEC_WAVE, instrument=LSF, name="spec")])
truth_pred = gen.predict(TRUTH)                    # AB maggies (phot), F_nu in cgs (spec)

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
mag = np.asarray(truth_pred["phot"]); mag_unc = mag / 20.0
sfx = np.asarray(truth_pred["spec"]); sfx_unc = np.abs(sfx) / 25.0
phot = Photometry(filters=FILTERS, name="phot", uncertainty=mag_unc,
                  flux=mag + mag_unc * rng.standard_normal(mag.shape))
spec = Spectrum(wavelength=SPEC_WAVE, instrument=LSF, name="spec", uncertainty=sfx_unc,
                flux=sfx + sfx_unc * rng.standard_normal(sfx.shape))
model = build_model([phot, spec])

Before fitting, use model.display() to inspect the parameters, priors, transforms and observations. The figure also compares the data with the range of model predictions allowed by the priors. model.latex() returns a LaTeX table of free, derived and fixed parameters, with their priors or values. The table requires \usepackage{booktabs,amsmath}.

fig, ax = model.display(return_fig=True)     # in a notebook, model.display() alone shows it
fig.savefig("model.png", dpi=150)
print(model.latex())

In a script, a bare model.display() opens a window and waits until you close it.

4. Fit with nested sampling. These settings are intended for a laptop. On an Apple Silicon Mac with macOS 26 and Python 3.12, the fit uses the GPU in float32 and takes about five minutes. Float64 CPU runs take somewhat longer; set JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu to use that mode on a Mac.

The example uses 60 inner slice steps. With the fitSED default of 30, the float32 GPU run gave a logmass posterior about 30% too narrow. The fit prints progress and saves ./my_fit/ceridwen_result.h5. For scientific use, increase num_live from this example's value; the fitSED default is 500. See Samplers for NUTS.

from ceridwen import fitSED

result = fitSED(
    model,
    sampler="nested",
    sampler_kwargs={"num_live": 100, "num_delete": 20, "num_inner_steps": 60,
                    "logZ_tol": -5.0},
    rng_key=jax.random.PRNGKey(42),
    output_dir="./my_fit",
)
print(f"log Z = {result.log_evidence:.2f} +/- {result.log_evidence_err:.2f}")

5. Inspect the result. PostProcess resamples the posterior to equal weight, evaluates the fitted model for those draws and computes derived quantities.

from ceridwen import PostProcess

pp  = PostProcess(model, result, n_samples=1000)
out = pp.run()

truth = {p: float(TRUTH[p][0]) for p in ("logzsol", "logmass", "diffuse_tau_kc", "diffuse_dust_index")}
for p, t in truth.items():
    lo, med, hi = np.percentile(out["theta"][p], [16, 50, 84])
    print(f"{p:>20}: true {t:+7.3f}   fit {med:+7.3f}  (-{med - lo:.3f}/+{hi - med:.3f})")

print(np.percentile(out["extras"]["sfh"]["sfr100"], [16, 50, 84]))   # SFR over 100 Myr [Msun/yr]
pp.figures("./my_fit/figures", title="mock galaxy",
           truths={**truth, "logsfr_ratios": np.asarray(TRUTH["logsfr_ratios"])})
pp.save("./my_fit/post.npz")

The table compares each posterior median and 16–84% interval with the input. Some recovered values differ from the input by 2–3 sigma. In this example, logmass is degenerate with the five-ratio SFH: mass in the oldest bins adds little light. A flat SFH with logmass=10.44 fits within 1 in ln L of the input, even without noise. The SFH prior favours that solution, giving a MAP of 10.44 rather than the input 10.50. On noise-free data with flat priors, the MAP is 10.498.

The 100-live-point runs also underestimate uncertainty. On the Apple GPU, this seed gives logmass=10.43 (−0.03/+0.03), and seed 0 gives 10.44 (−0.03/+0.03). The float64 CPU run gives 10.44 (−0.02/+0.03). Increase num_live before using these intervals. The five SFH ratios are mostly prior-dominated, and one or two may fall outside their 95% intervals.

figures writes summary.pdf (SED, residuals, SFH and marginals), corner.pdf and diagnostics.pdf. post.npz stores predictions for every draw and is about 100 MB; reload it with load_postprocess. See Post-processing for the output fields.

docs.title: Reloading a fit
docs.text: load_result_h5("my_fit/ceridwen_result.h5"), imported from ceridwen, reloads the result in a later session. Reconstruct the model with the same grid, CSP, observations and transforms. ceridwen.resultfile.rebuild_model(path, csp, observations, transforms=...) reads the priors, free parameters, redshift and kinematics from the file and checks the reconstructed model against the saved configuration. check_model_against_result(model, path) lists differences. You can also pass the file path directly to PostProcess(model, "my_fit/ceridwen_result.h5").

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Photometry predictions use AB maggies. Spectrum predictions use observed-frame F_nu in erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² Hz⁻¹; multiply by 1e32 to convert to nJy. Lines predictions are integrated fluxes in erg s⁻¹ cm⁻². Set zred= or lumdist_mpc= on SedModel to obtain these fluxes. At zred=0 without a luminosity distance, the model applies no flux factor and issues a warning. See Conventions for details and the Tutorial for emission lines and nebular emission (add_neb=True).

docs.title: Samplers
docs.text:
fitSED(model, sampler=...) supports nested sampling and NUTS, with optional VI preconditioning for NUTS. Each uses the same log-posterior and returns a SamplingResult compatible with PostProcess, plotting and result files. The examples use model from the Quick start.

sampler sampler= gradients evidence on a laptop CPU nested sampling (default) "nested" (or "ns", "nss") no yes, result.log_evidence minutes to tens of minutes NUTS "nuts" (or "hmc") yes no hours; use a GPU VI-preconditioned NUTS "nuts" with vi="tril" or vi="iaf" yes no hours; use a GPU

docs.title: Nested sampling
docs.text:
Nested sampling is the default. It draws live points from the prior, uses no gradients and estimates the Bayesian evidence (log Z). Every free parameter requires a proper prior.

import jax
from ceridwen import fitSED

result = fitSED(
    model,
    sampler="nested",
    sampler_kwargs={"num_live": 400, "num_delete": 80, "logZ_tol": -5.0},
    rng_key=jax.random.PRNGKey(42),
    output_dir="./my_fit",
)
print(f"log Z = {result.log_evidence:.2f} +/- {result.log_evidence_err:.2f}")

Pass these settings in sampler_kwargs:

  • num_live: number of live points, default 500. Increasing this generally improves posterior resolution and evidence precision at a proportional cost.
  • num_delete: points replaced per iteration, default num_live // 5.
  • num_inner_steps: MCMC steps per replacement, default 30.
  • logZ_tol: stopping threshold for the remaining evidence, ln(Z_live / Z), default −5.
  • slice_kernel: "lanes" (default), "stock" or "carry".

"stock" uses blackjax.nss unchanged. "carry" evaluates each stepping-out edge once rather than twice under vmap. "lanes" runs replacement chains in a shared loop, skips likelihood evaluation for candidates below the prior slice level and uses idle batch slots to evaluate candidates in advance. It implements Dance et al. (2025, arXiv:2503.17405), with code by Liu Hao (@potatoist314).

"carry" and "lanes" use the same random numbers and evaluations as "stock". On CPUs, "carry" is bitwise identical to "stock". "lanes" is bitwise identical on Apple Silicon; on x86, XLA's arithmetic ordering introduces differences in the last bits. Long x86 runs can consequently follow different trajectories while agreeing statistically.

There is one intentional difference with blackjax 1.6. When all moves in a replacement chain are rejected, "lanes" assigns the replacement particle the birth contour of the particle it replaces. Blackjax 1.7 uses the same rule. Version 1.6 retained the starting particle's birth contour, which can bias ln Z on a flat likelihood. This affects weights and evidence only for chains without an accepted move.

GPU arithmetic can produce different trajectories as batch composition changes. Runs need not be bitwise reproducible across processes, including two "stock" runs with the same key on A100s. Compare their results statistically.

For a 19-parameter JADES photometry and emission-line model with num_live=300 and num_delete=64, "lanes" was 3.5–3.8 times faster than "stock" on an A100. Posteriors agreed, and ln Z differed by at most 2e-5. A single measurement on a busy 11-core laptop CPU gave a sevenfold speedup per iteration.

The progress bar counts dead points. Runtime grows with num_live. On a shared 11-core laptop CPU, the Quick start model with num_live=100, num_delete=20 and logZ_tol=-2.0 took 12 minutes with "lanes" and 21–29 minutes with "stock". Both used 67,800 likelihood calls. With 400 live points, "stock" processed about 1.3 dead points per second and took hours.

docs.title: Checkpoints and resuming
docs.text:
Set checkpoint_dir= or $CERIDWEN_CHECKPOINT_DIR to save ns_checkpoint_<pid>.pkl periodically. checkpoint_interval_s defaults to 1200 seconds. To resume an interrupted run, pass the checkpoint as resume_from= with the same rng_key and settings. It restores the live and dead points and can reproduce an uninterrupted run.

Loading checks the settings, parameter shapes and live-point log-likelihoods (relative tolerance 1e-6) against the model. You may change slice_kernel when resuming because the kernels use the same moves and random numbers, subject to the numerical and version differences described above.

result = fitSED(model, sampler="nested", output_dir="./my_fit",
                rng_key=jax.random.PRNGKey(42),
                sampler_kwargs={"checkpoint_dir": "./ckpt",
                                "resume_from": "./ckpt/ns_checkpoint_12345.pkl"})

docs.title: NUTS
docs.text:
The No-U-Turn sampler uses gradients from the JAX forward model. It is suited to GPU fits with many parameters. Defaults are 4 chains, 2000 samples per chain, 1500 warmup steps, a dense mass matrix and target acceptance 0.95. Bounded parameters are automatically mapped to an unconstrained space.

result = fitSED(
    model,
    sampler="nuts",
    sampler_kwargs={"num_chains": 4, "num_samples": 2000},
    rng_key=jax.random.PRNGKey(42),
    output_dir="./my_fit",
)

Warmup and sampling each run as a compiled loop without progress output. Ctrl-C does not interrupt a loop; stop the process with kill. An interrupted NUTS run does not save a result.

docs.title: VI-preconditioned NUTS
docs.text:
Variational inference fits a transport map before NUTS samples in the transformed space (Hoffman et al. 2019). Use vi="tril" for a full-rank Gaussian or vi="iaf" for an inverse autoregressive flow (NeuTra). With VI, warmup defaults to 200 steps and a diagonal mass matrix.

result = fitSED(
    model,
    sampler="nuts",
    vi="tril",
    sampler_kwargs={"num_chains": 4, "num_samples": 2000},
    rng_key=jax.random.PRNGKey(42),
    output_dir="./my_fit",
)

# VI convergence: -ELBO should drop and then plateau. It can be negative (the likelihood is
# normalised), so the axis is linear.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.figure(); plt.plot(result.raw["vi_losses"])
plt.xlabel("VI iteration"); plt.ylabel(r"$-\mathrm{ELBO}$")
plt.savefig("vi_losses.png")

docs.title: Starting at the MAP
docs.text:
fitSED(..., optimize=True) first finds a MAP estimate using L-BFGS (ceridwen.optimize.map_fit). It starts from model.theta_init and n_starts prior draws. NUTS and its VI map start from the MAP; nested sampling still draws live points from the prior. Both save the MAP under /map in the result file. You can also call map_fit(model) separately and pass the returned MAPResult.theta as free_param_init.

from ceridwen.optimize import map_fit

best = map_fit(model, n_starts=16, rng_key=jax.random.PRNGKey(1))
result = fitSED(model, sampler="nuts", optimize=True,
                optimize_kwargs={"n_starts": 16}, output_dir="./my_fit")

docs.title: NUTS on a CPU: measured times
docs.text:
These measurements used the Quick start model: twelve photometric bands, a 600-pixel spectrum and nine free parameters. They ran on shared 11-core laptop CPUs with other jobs active, so use them as approximate timings.

run measured map_fit(model, n_starts=16) 108.5 s VI-preconditioned NUTS (vi="tril"), 4 x 2000 VI 72 s; warmup 596 s (200 steps, step size 0.0017); sampling not finished after 1 h 54 min NUTS after the MAP (optimize=True), 4 x 2000 not finished after 80 min

Nested sampling is generally the practical choice on a CPU; NUTS benefits from a GPU.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Run the environment check first. It checks Python, dependencies, filter curves, attenuation laws, float64, nested sampling and $SPS_HOME, and suggests fixes for any problems:

python -m ceridwen.check

pip reports "No matching distribution found for jaxlib>=0.9.0" on a Mac. This usually means Python is an Intel (x86_64) build. JAX has no Intel-Mac wheels after 0.4.38, while CERIDWEN requires JAX >= 0.9. On Apple Silicon, an older Intel Anaconda installation running under Rosetta can cause this. Check Python's architecture with:

python -c "import platform; print(platform.machine())"     # must print arm64

If it prints x86_64, install Miniforge for arm64 and create the environment with its conda. Intel Macs cannot run CERIDWEN.

$SPS_HOME is unset or incomplete. CSPBasis(add_neb=True) and add_dust_emission=True require either sps_home= or $SPS_HOME. Clone FSPS and add the path to your shell startup file; see Installation. Open a new terminal and run echo $SPS_HOME. If it is blank, check that you edited the startup file for your shell (echo $SHELL).

python-fsps fails to import. The wrapper is needed only for SSPData.from_fsps, which builds SSP grids. Set $SPS_HOME and install a Fortran compiler before installing it. See Building a grid.

A cached grid fails its checksum. The file in ~/.ceridwen/grids or $CERIDWEN_GRID_DIR may be incomplete or from an earlier release. Download a replacement with fetch_grid(name, force=True).

Python imports the wrong ceridwen. Running from the directory containing a clone can cause Python to find that folder before the installed package. Run the script from inside the clone or another directory.

NUTS produces no output for a long time. Warmup and sampling each run as a compiled loop without progress output. Ctrl-C does not interrupt these loops; use kill to stop the process. Typical CPU fits take hours. Use nested sampling on the CPU or run NUTS on a GPU; see Samplers.

Grid-dependent tests are skipped. These tests cannot run without an SSP grid. Point them at the published BPASS grid:

export CERIDWEN_TEST_SSP=$(python -c "from ceridwen.ssps import fetch_grid; print(fetch_grid('mist_bpass_v2'))")

Results have unexpected values. Check metallicity units (logzsol is log10(Z/Z_sun) for the loaded grid), lookback-time ordering (index 0 is today) and spelling of theta keys. See Conventions and GOTCHAS.md. If you use an AI assistant, give it the repository's AGENTS.md instructions.

docs.title: Tutorial: fitting photometry, spectroscopy and lines jointly
docs.text:
CERIDWEN can fit broadband photometry, resolved spectra and emission-line fluxes separately or together. Each observation object projects the forward model into the appropriate data space. The joint likelihood combines the individual observation likelihoods.

This tutorial constructs one observation of each type and fits them jointly. Replace the mock arrays with your data when using it for a real fit.

Example scripts

examples/demo_2_photometry_lines.py fits photometry and line fluxes. examples/demo_3_spectrum_advanced.py fits photometry and a spectrum with an Instrument, sampled sigma_gal, line masking and a noise floor.

Requirements

See Conventions and common errors for metallicity (logzsol = log10(Z/Z_sun) for the loaded grid) and lookback-time ordering (index 0 is today). Set up FSPS and $SPS_HOME as described in Installation. Nebular continuum and lines require the FSPS CLOUDY grids.

docs.title: 1. Build the forward model
docs.text:
Set add_neb=True to include lines and nebular continuum. This example also enables diffuse and birth-cloud dust attenuation.

import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

from ceridwen import SSPData, CSPBasis, SedModel, fitSED, Kinematics, Instrument, Cosmology
from ceridwen.observation import Photometry, Spectrum, Lines
from ceridwen.priors import Uniform, ClippedNormal, StudentT
from ceridwen.model import logsfr_ratios_to_sfh

ssp = SSPData.load("ssp_data.h5")          # built once via SSPData.from_fsps(...)
# The grid records its isochrone library; CSPBasis reads it automatically,
# so isoc_type never needs to be passed in init_neb_params.

ZRED = 0.5                                  # spectroscopic redshift of the galaxy

# The cosmology is a property of the analysis: choose it once, here, and every
# distance and age in the fit comes from it.  Presets: Cosmology.planck18(),
# planck15(), wmap9() (prospector's); Cosmology.flat(H0, Om0) for the two
# numbers a paper quotes; Cosmology.from_astropy(...) for any flat astropy
# cosmology.  CSPBasis requires it; SedModel reads it from the CSP.
cosmo = Cosmology.planck18()

# lookback_time is the static SFH node grid (Gyr, increasing, index 0 = today,
# >= 2 nodes). Its oldest node must not exceed the age of the universe at ZRED,
# cosmo.age(0.5) = 8.6 Gyr under Planck18; SedModel refuses a grid that does.
# CSPBasis refuses to build without a grid (or an explicit theta).
lookback = jnp.linspace(0.0, 8.0, 5)        # 5 nodes -> 4 free logsfr_ratios
csp = CSPBasis(
    ssp,
    lookback_time=lookback,
    cosmo=cosmo,
    zh_const=True, sfh_interp="step",       # one "logzsol"; zh_const=False samples "logzsol_hist"
    add_dust=True, add_diffuse_dust=True,   # birth-cloud + diffuse attenuation
    add_neb=True,                           # nebular continuum + lines (needs $SPS_HOME)
    add_igm=True,                           # Madau (1995), auto-scales with zred
    # sps_home defaults to $SPS_HOME
)

Set the galaxy's velocity dispersions on the model through Kinematics, which is shared by all observations. Here the stellar dispersion is sampled and the gas dispersion is tied to it:

kin = Kinematics(sigma_gal="sigma_gal")     # free (theta key); sigma_gas tied to sigma_gal
# Kinematics(sigma_gal=250.0, sigma_gas="sigma_gas")   stars fixed, gas free
# Kinematics(sigma_gal=300.0)                          both fixed (the SedModel default)

With sampled sigma_gas, emission lines are placed on the model grid and broadened at each likelihood call. This also applies when the gas width is tied to sampled sigma_gal, as here. Fixed gas width, for example Kinematics(sigma_gal="sigma_gal", sigma_gas=150.0), allows photometry to use a faster static line-to-band matrix. Sampled redshift requires line profiles to be recomputed. See Conventions.

docs.title: 2. Photometry
docs.text:
Supply broadband fluxes in AB maggies. Filter names refer to CERIDWEN's bundled library of 293 filters; list them with python -c "from ceridwen.observation.filters import list_available_filters as f; print(f())". The photometric prediction includes continuum and lines without the aperture or spectral calibration factors discussed below.

# If your catalogue is in nJy (common for JWST), convert to maggies and apply a
# small error floor (here 5%), as the JADES pipeline does:
flux_nJy, unc_nJy = my_phot_nJy, my_phot_unc_nJy
unc_nJy = np.where(unc_nJy / flux_nJy > 0.05, unc_nJy, 0.05 * flux_nJy)

phot = Photometry(
    filters=["jwst_f090w", "jwst_f115w", "jwst_f150w", "jwst_f200w",
             "jwst_f277w", "jwst_f356w", "jwst_f444w"],
    flux=jnp.asarray(flux_nJy) * 1e-9 / 3631.0,        # nJy -> AB maggies
    uncertainty=jnp.asarray(unc_nJy) * 1e-9 / 3631.0,
    name="phot",                    # the key this observation is reported under
)

Optional boolean arrays are mask= (True includes a band) and upper_limit= (True marks a non-detection for the one-sided χ² penalty).

docs.title: 3. Spectrum
docs.text:
Supply observed-frame vacuum wavelengths in Å and observed-frame F_ν in erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² Hz⁻¹. One nJy is 1e-32 in these units. The model is redshifted onto the supplied pixels; at zred=0, rest and observed frames coincide.

Attach the line-spread function using Instrument. Its constructor specifies both the unit and resolving-power convention: R = λ/FWHM in most datasheets, or R = λ/σ in sedpy/Prospector. These differ by a factor of about 2.35, so there is no constructor taking an unspecified R.

For schema-2 grids, library resolution is subtracted in quadrature from the instrumental width at each pixel. Galaxy velocity dispersion comes from the model's Kinematics and is combined with the instrument during projection.

spec = Spectrum(
    wavelength=my_obs_wave_aa,      # Å, vacuum, OBSERVED frame, shape (n_pix,)
    flux=my_spec_fnu,               # F_nu per pixel, erg s^-1 cm^-2 Hz^-1 (cgs)
    uncertainty=my_spec_unc,
    instrument=Instrument.sigma_kms(120.0),   # LSF: sigma in km/s
    # Instrument.R_fwhm(2700)                 # datasheet R = lambda/FWHM
    # Instrument.R_sigma(6358)                # sedpy / Prospector R = lambda/sigma (= R_fwhm(2700))
    # Instrument.fwhm_aa(2.5)                 # FWHM in Angstrom, observed frame
    # Instrument.R_fwhm(R_arr, wave=my_obs_wave_aa)   # per-pixel curve (prism)
    # Instrument.R_fwhm(2700, scale="lsf_scale")      # LSF width x a free scale (bounded
    #                                   prior + free_param_init; docs/conventions.md)
    # subtract_library=True (default): the SSP library resolution is removed
    # in quadrature; False only for a grid whose stored curve you distrust.
    noise_floor=0.01,               # 1% multiplicative calibration floor (optional)
    name="spec",
)

# Optional: mask known emission lines from the *continuum* spectrum fit so they
# do not double-count against the Lines object, redshifting line centres first.
spec.mask_lines([4862.76, 5008.31, 6564.72], dv=500.0, zred=ZRED)   # vacuum rest

You can also pass a fixed per-pixel multiplicative calibration= vector and mask=. Where the instrument is finer than the SSP library, the continuum remains at library resolution. A warning reports the affected pixel count and range. If this affects the whole spectrum despite a high-resolution grid, check the Instrument units.

docs.title: 4. Emission lines
docs.text:
Supply integrated line fluxes. line_ind contains indices into the FSPS emlines_info.dat list; wavelength contains vacuum rest wavelengths in Å. The model matches nebular lines by wavelength within 1 Å and raises an error if no match exists. Indices are checked against that match, with a warning on disagreement.

# Catalogue line fluxes are often quoted in 1e-20 erg s^-1 cm^-2; scale to
# absolute CGS to match the model (adjust the factor to your catalogue).
LINE_UNIT = 1.0e-20

lines = Lines(
    line_ind=[59, 61, 62, 74, 75],                         # Hβ, [OIII]4959/5007, Hα, [NII]6584
    line_names=["Hbeta", "[OIII]4959", "[OIII]5007", "Halpha", "[NII]6583"],
    wavelength=[4862.76, 4960.37, 5008.31, 6564.72, 6585.37],  # Å, vacuum rest
    flux=np.asarray(my_line_flux) * LINE_UNIT,             # erg s^-1 cm^-2
    uncertainty=np.asarray(my_line_unc) * LINE_UNIT,
    name="lines",
)

A Lines prediction starts from the nebular grid luminosity and applies dust attenuation, mass and distance scaling, and IGM transmission. IGM transmission is averaged over the model-grid profile, which matters for Ly-α because the Madau forest begins within the line. Integrated fluxes do not depend on Kinematics or Instrument. Models with add_neb=False, including CSPBasis_afe, reject Lines observations with ValueError.

Flux calibration: eline_scaling and spectrum_scaling

Aperture losses or calibration errors may put line fluxes and spectra on a different scale from the photometry. Two parameters handle this:

  • eline_scaling multiplies only Lines predictions. A value of 0.65 gives 65% of the predicted line flux. It does not affect a Spectrum.
  • spectrum_scaling multiplies the entire Spectrum prediction, including lines, relative to the photometric flux scale. This follows Prospector's spec_norm convention.

Neither changes photometry. Add a prior for each factor you want to fit.

Wavelength-dependent calibration: spectrum_calib

A single scale factor cannot describe wavelength-dependent calibration errors from throughput, differential refraction or aperture colour terms. spectrum_calib supplies Legendre coefficients c_1 .. c_order for the multiplicative response 1 + sum_k c_k P_k(x). Here x maps all observed pixel wavelengths to [-1, 1]. There is no c_0 term because spectrum_scaling sets the level. The combined response is spectrum_scaling * (1 + sum_k c_k P_k(x)).

This resembles Prospector's polyorder and pPXF's mdegree, with coefficients sampled rather than solved analytically. Including photometry helps constrain the continuum shape. Orders 2–6 are typical; higher orders may fit real features such as the 4000 Å break or broad molecular bands. Inspect the fitted response. A single prior is broadcast over the coefficient vector:

priors["spectrum_calib"] = Uniform(low=-0.2, high=0.2)
free_param_init["spectrum_calib"] = jnp.zeros(4)      # order 4

Without spectrum_calib in theta, its factor is one. The implementation is in ceridwen/csp/spectrum_calibration.py, applied by _project_observations in both CSPBasis and CSPBasis_afe.

For several spectra, use spectrum_scaling_<obs.name> and spectrum_calib_<obs.name>. Unsuffixed names are accepted only when there is exactly one spectrum; otherwise SedModel raises an error.

Profiled polynomial: Spectrum(polynomial_order=M)

Spectrum(..., polynomial_order=3) multiplies the model by 1 + sum_{m=0}^{3} c_m T_m(x), using Chebyshev polynomials over the unmasked wavelength range. A weighted least-squares solve finds the maximum-likelihood coefficients at every call, as in Prospector's PolyOptCal. The calculation is differentiable and adds no sampled parameters.

Weights are 1/sigma_eff^2, including noise terms. Prospector uses the quoted 1/sigma^2, so results agree when no noise terms are active. T_0 sets the level; spectrum_scaling and spectrum_calib for that spectrum are therefore rejected. polynomial_regularization= adds a ridge term. The posterior is conditional on the fitted polynomial and omits its uncertainty. PostProcess returns each draw's response in out["prediction"]["calibration"][name] and applies it to predictions.

Marginalised calibration polynomial

The model depends linearly on polynomial coefficients. With Gaussian priors, these can be integrated out analytically:

spec = Spectrum(..., polynomial_order=6, polynomial_mode="marginalize",
                polynomial_prior_sigma=0.1)     # float, or one width per T_0..T_6

Using the same Chebyshev basis, response 1 + sum_m c_m T_m(x) and priors c_m ~ N(0, s_m^2), the marginal likelihood is

ln L = ln L_diag(y - mu) + 1/2 b^T M^-1 b - 1/2 ln|M| - 1/2 ln|Lambda|,

M = D^T W D + Lambda^-1, b = D^T W (y - mu), D = diag(mu) A, Lambda = diag(s^2).

The calculation costs O(n k^2) per call and adds no sampled parameters. Calibration uncertainty is propagated into the posterior and evidence. The prior width s is in fractional-response units: 0.1 allows roughly 10% calibration errors per term. Set s_m=0 to fix a coefficient at zero. An infinite width is rejected because it leaves the marginal likelihood undefined.

  • T_0 sets the overall scale and is degenerate with mass unless photometry or a fixed calibration constrains the level. To sample spectrum_scaling instead, fix T_0 with polynomial_prior_sigma=[0.0, s_1, ..., s_M]. Other sampled calibration terms for that spectrum are rejected.
  • polynomial_regularization is available only in profiled mode. Here the prior width supplies the constraint; reg_m = 1/s_m gives the same best-fitting polynomial as the conditional mean.
  • The same spectrum cannot use an outlier mixture, upper limits, logify_spectrum=True, GP noise or marginalize_elines=True. These invalidate the assumed Gaussian linear model; jointly scaling line and polynomial coefficients makes it bilinear.
  • W uses the noise model's 1/sigma_eff^2 at the uncalibrated model, as in profiled mode. This is exact when the variance has no model-dependent terms.
  • PostProcess returns the conditional-mean response in out["prediction"]["calibration"][name] and applies it to spectra[name]. out["extras"]["calibration"][name] contains per-draw mean, sd, cov and draws. The last contains one draw from each conditional Gaussian, together sampling the marginal coefficient posterior. The result file records mode, order and prior widths in read_result_h5(path)["obs"][name]["likelihood"]["poly_calibration"].

Profiling and marginalisation both cost O(n k^2). Sampling is cheaper per likelihood call but adds M + 1 parameters. The following CPU measurements used float64 and jit(vmap) over W draws on a shared Apple machine, with about ±20% timing variation (scripts/bench_poly_marginal.py). Units are microseconds per batch:

W M profile marginalize sampled spectrum likelihood only (2000 px), value + grad 32 1 916 905 177 32 3 900 943 294 32 6 2249 2298 288 32 10 3521 3878 297 32 20 5006 6328 356 full log-posterior (forward model, 1000 px), value + grad 1 3 2372 2173 2591 1 20 2262 2616 2160 32 1 65090 65246 64855 32 3 67722 66507 69782 32 6 71060 70132 70526 32 10 70523 70375 81709 32 20 66412 65540 65974

In the full log-posterior, the forward model dominated runtime and differences between calibration methods were within timing variation at every tested order. Sampling still adds dimensions as the order increases. GPU timings at production batch width W = 100 have not been measured. Code is in ceridwen/likelihood/poly_marginal.py.

docs.title: 5. Priors and the model
docs.text:
Collect the observations into one list. Include only the types you are fitting, using empty lists for the others, and give each free parameter a prior.

observations = [phot, spec, lines]

priors = {
    # Stellar population. logzsol = log10(Z/Z_sun); MIST grids span [-2.50, +0.50].
    # Birth-cloud dust ("tau_pow", "alpha_pow" for the powerlaw law) and every
    # other registered parameter needs a prior: print csp.param_names.
    "logzsol":           ClippedNormal(mean=-0.3, sigma=0.5, low=-2.0, high=0.2),
    "logmass":           Uniform(low=7.0, high=12.5),
    "logsfr_ratios":     StudentT(df=2.0, mean=0.0, scale=0.3),   # non-parametric SFH
    # Dust.
    "diffuse_tau_kc":    ClippedNormal(mean=0.3, sigma=1.0, low=0.0, high=4.0),
    "diffuse_dust_index": Uniform(low=-1.0, high=0.4),
    "tau_pow":           ClippedNormal(mean=0.3, sigma=0.5, low=0.0, high=4.0),
    "alpha_pow":         ClippedNormal(mean=-1.0, sigma=0.5, low=-2.5, high=0.5),
    # Nebular (required for the Lines / nebular continuum).
    "gas_logz":          Uniform(low=-1.3, high=0.2),   # inside the CLOUDY axis
    "gas_logu":          Uniform(low=-4.0, high=-1.0),
    # Emission-line aperture correction (Lines observation only).
    "eline_scaling":     Uniform(low=0.1, high=2.0),
    # Spectrophotometric normalisation of the spectrum onto the photometry
    # (Spectrum observation only; independent of eline_scaling). Omit if the
    # spectrum is already flux-calibrated to the photometric system.
    "spectrum_scaling":         ClippedNormal(mean=1.0, sigma=0.3, low=0.2, high=3.0),
    # Stellar velocity dispersion [km/s], the free key named in Kinematics above.
    # The upper bound must stay below Kinematics.sigma_max (2000 by default).
    "sigma_gal":         Uniform(low=20.0, high=600.0),
}

# The non-parametric SFH is sampled as logsfr_ratios and turned into the per-bin
# sfh by a REGISTERED transform; this step is required for logsfr_ratios to work.
sfh_times_yr = np.array(csp.sfh_times)
def logsfr_to_sfh(free_theta, _t=sfh_times_yr):
    return logsfr_ratios_to_sfh(free_theta["logsfr_ratios"], sfh_times_yr=_t)

N_RATIOS = 4   # number of SFH nodes - 1
model = SedModel(
    csp,
    observations=observations,
    priors=priors,
    transforms={"sfh": logsfr_to_sfh},        # REQUIRED for logsfr_ratios
    free_param_init={"logsfr_ratios": jnp.zeros(N_RATIOS),
                     "logmass": jnp.array([10.0]),
                     "sigma_gal": jnp.array([150.0]),
                     "eline_scaling": jnp.array([1.0]),      # sampled nuisances that are
                     "spectrum_scaling": jnp.array([1.0])},  # not CSP parameters need a start value
    zred=ZRED,                                # fixed spectroscopic redshift
    kinematics=kin,                           # galaxy dispersions (default: Kinematics(sigma_gal=300.0))
    broaden_photometry=True,                  # photometry sees the sigma_gal-broadened spectrum (default)
)

SedModel validates Kinematics before compilation. It rejects missing free keys, fixed widths also present in theta, and bounded priors above sigma_max. A sampled key without a prior produces a warning. Omitting kinematics= uses DEFAULT_KINEMATICS, or Kinematics(sigma_gal=300.0) for both stars and gas. The summary reports these values.

To fit redshift, add zred to free_param_init with a bounded prior such as Uniform or ClippedNormal. For a non-parametric SFH, construct the CSP with track_zred_age=True. It stretches the SFH grid to age(zred) and scales SFR by T_grid / age(zred) to preserve mass. Keep the transform logsfr_ratios_to_sfh(..., sfh_times_yr=csp.sfh_times); logmass then represents formed mass at every redshift. PostProcess reports each draw's SFR on its own age grid with mass_formed = 10**logmass.

All observations follow sampled redshift. Flux scaling, IGM transmission and line fluxes use theta["zred"], and photometry is projected through filters at that redshift. The spectral projector covers the full prior range, reads the model at each redshift and places lines at lambda_rest (1 + z). Set Spectrum(zred_range=(z_min, z_max)) if the prior lacks finite bounds or a transform supplies redshift.

The projector extends the fixed-redshift log grid around the initial zred value. At that value, free- and fixed-redshift projections agree exactly. Elsewhere, interpolation occurs at a different grid phase, causing differences at roughly the per-mille level for a MILES-resolution grid. The library width in the fixed kernel remains that of the initial redshift; build warns if it would vary by more than 10%.

The redshift derivative follows the linear interpolation and is piecewise constant between log-grid nodes, on a scale of about 1e-8 in z, below the scale NUTS resolves. Use a prior as narrow as the data justify. The projector's window must fit inside the model grid throughout the range.

docs.title: 6. Fit
docs.text:
fitSED constructs a joint likelihood from model.observations, with one Gaussian likelihood per observation name, and saves an HDF5 result.

result = fitSED(
    model,
    observations,
    sampler="nested",               # or "nuts" (optionally vi="tril")
    rng_key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
    output_dir="./joint_fit",
)

print(f"ln Z = {result.log_evidence:.2f} +/- {result.log_evidence_err:.2f}")

fitSED(model, observations) replaces the model's observations and calls model.setup_observations(). If you assign model.observations directly, call setup yourself before prediction or fitting.

docs.title: 7. Posterior and diagnostics
docs.text:
from ceridwen import PostProcess

pp  = PostProcess(model, result, n_samples=2000)   # equal-weight draws, nested weights recomputed
out = pp.run()
print("median logmass:", float(np.median(out["theta"]["logmass"])))

out["prediction"]["photometry"]["phot"]      # posterior-predictive maggies (draws x bands)
out["prediction"]["spectra"][spec.name]      # posterior-predictive spectrum (draws x pixels)
out["prediction"]["lines"][lines.name]       # posterior-predictive line fluxes
out["bestfit"]["theta"]                      # the maximum-likelihood sample
out["extras"]["sfh"]["sfr10"]                # derived quantities

# Summary (SED + chi, line residuals, SFH, marginals), corner and sampling
# diagnostics for this galaxy:
pp.figures("./joint_fit/figures", title="joint fit")
pp.save("./joint_fit/post.npz")

result.samples contains raw samples keyed by parameter name. The HDF5 file stores observations, priors, samples and nested-sampling evidence. Pass the file to PostProcess(model, "joint_fit/ceridwen_result.h5") to reload it. See Post-processing for its fields and examples/demo_3_spectrum_advanced.py for a photometry-and-spectrum script.

docs.title: Checks before fitting data
docs.text:
• Put photometry in maggies, spectra in cgs F_ν and line fluxes in erg s⁻¹ cm⁻². Their calibrations must correspond to the same model normalisation at zred. Inconsistent calibrations can give acceptable separate fits but a poor joint fit.
  • When fitting line fluxes measured from the same spectrum, mask those lines in the spectrum with spec.mask_lines(...) to avoid counting their measurements twice.
  • Use eline_scaling for Lines aperture losses and spectrum_scaling for the spectral calibration relative to photometry. Fit whichever factors are needed. A fixed per-pixel calibration vector can correct known calibration differences; noise_floor accounts for additional uncertainty.
  • Set galaxy dispersions through Kinematics and instrumental widths through each spectrum's Instrument. If sigma_gal reaches a prior boundary, check whether resolving power was supplied as R_FWHM or R_sigma; confusing them changes the width by a factor of 2.35.
  • Spectral pixels use observed-frame vacuum Å. Line-list wavelengths and mask_lines(..., zred=z) centres use rest-frame vacuum Å. mask_lines shifts centres by the supplied (1 + zred); omitting redshift gives a warning and uses zero.
